candidates.source_name: Ephrem the Syrian / Commentary on Exodus
candidates.source_attribution: Ephrem the Syrian, Commentary on Exodus II.2 (NPNF S2 V13, Gwynn/Schaff trans., Oxford 1898). PD.
candidates.draft_body:
Ephrem the Syrian Commentary on Exodus (c. 360 AD)

When the mother of Moses sees that her child is 'goodly' (asteios), Ephrem reads this not as physical beauty alone but as divinely-bestowed countenance, a foreshadowing of the 'fairest of the sons of men' (Ps 45:2). The radiance her eyes detect is the same radiance that will shine from Moses' face at Sinai and from the face of Christ at the Transfiguration.

candidates.source_name: Ephrem the Syrian / Sermo de Domino Nostro
candidates.source_attribution: Ephrem the Syrian, Sermo de Domino Nostro 3-4 (NPNF S2 V13). PD.
candidates.draft_body:
Ephrem the Syrian Sermo de Domino Nostro (c. 363 AD)

The three-month hiding of the infant Moses, ended by his being laid in an ark of bulrushes pitched with bitumen, is for Ephrem the first Pascal typology of the Old Testament: the ark is the tomb, the three months are the days of burial in cipher, and the deliverer is preserved through the very waters that should have destroyed him. Tewahedo carries this reading as part of its Pascal lectionary catechesis: Moses-in-the-ark anticipates Christ-in-the-tomb.

candidates.source_name: Ephrem the Syrian / Commentary on Exodus
candidates.source_attribution: Ephrem the Syrian, Commentary on Exodus II.5 (NPNF S2 V13, Gwynn/Schaff trans., Oxford 1898). PD.
candidates.draft_body:
Ephrem the Syrian Commentary on Exodus (c. 360 AD)

Pharaoh's daughter, drawing the Hebrew infant out of the river and giving him a name, is for Ephrem the first prefiguration of the Gentile Church receiving the Word from among the Hebrews. The Egyptian princess does what her father refuses to do; the daughter of the oppressor saves the deliverer of the oppressed. Tewahedo cites this as a canonical anchor for Gentile-incorporation into the people of God.

candidates.source_name: Ephrem the Syrian / Commentary on Exodus
candidates.source_attribution: Ephrem the Syrian, Commentary on Exodus II.10 (NPNF S2 V13, Gwynn/Schaff trans., Oxford 1898). PD.
candidates.draft_body:
Ephrem the Syrian Commentary on Exodus (c. 360 AD)

Moses meeting Zipporah at the well in Midian, after defending her father's flock from hostile shepherds, is read by Ephrem as the second well-betrothal after Jacob and Rachel: a prophet meeting his bride at a well of living water. The pattern recurs at Sychar, where the true Bridegroom meets the Samaritan woman at Jacob's well (Jn 4). Tewahedo treats Ex 2:21 as a canonical link in the well-betrothal chain culminating in the Bridegroom-Christ.

Pharaoh's daughter, drawing the Hebrew infant out of the river and giving him a name, is for Ephrem the first prefiguration of the Gentile Church receiving the Word from among the Hebrews. The Egyptian princess does what her father refuses to do; the daughter of the oppressor saves the deliverer of the oppressed. Tewahedo cites this as a canonical anchor for Gentile-incorporation into the people of God.

Ephrem the Syrian Commentary on Exodus (c. 360 AD)

Moses meeting Zipporah at the well in Midian, after defending her father's flock from hostile shepherds, is read by Ephrem as the second well-betrothal after Jacob and Rachel: a prophet meeting his bride at a well of living water. The pattern recurs at Sychar, where the true Bridegroom meets the Samaritan woman at Jacob's well (Jn 4). Tewahedo treats Ex 2:21 as a canonical link in the well-betrothal chain culminating in the Bridegroom-Christ.
